solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Ugandans yell out words in friendly celebration

indicators.note: Letters that are 'out' have come loose from their places and can be rearranged.

explanation.surface: A crowd of Ugandans shouting at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: The linked answer spans 1, 16 and 21. 'Yell out' looks like one verb phrase, but 'yell' belongs to the fodder and 'out' alone does the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Auld Lang Syne is the Scottish song sung in friendship at New Year and other celebrations.

clue.text: Fellow fearless but no good as a high-up civil servant?

indicators.note: 'No good' tells you to take away G, the abbreviation for good.

blocks.note: G is the usual abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a bold man lacking goodness could be a senior official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fearless but no good' reads as a character sketch, but 'no good' is an instruction to drop G, the abbreviation for good.
explanation.definitionFit: Mandarin is the British term for a powerful senior civil servant, borrowed from the officials of imperial China.

clue.text: Queen sitting on rug maybe, squashing a small insect

indicators.note: ER squashes A between its letters, holding it inside.
In a down answer, what sits on something comes above it, so the queen goes before the rug.

explanation.surface: A queen perched on a carpet crushes a bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rug maybe' is not a carpet but slang for a hairpiece, WIG. ER is the Queen by the royal cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by kind: the earwig is a common garden insect, not much more than an inch long.

clue.text: I had rolled over on top of small building and fallen off

indicators.note: Something rolled over ends up the other way round, so ID becomes DI.
In a down answer the part on top comes first.

blocks.note: I'd is short for I had
a shed is a small building

explanation.surface: Someone describes rolling off the top of a small building and falling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small building' looks like a single unit, but 'small' gives MINI and 'building' gives SHED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has fallen off, as sales or attendance do, has diminished.

clue.text: Beside a road there is dirty handkerchief

indicators.note: 'Beside' puts FOUL next to A RD, one after the other.

blocks.note: RD is the abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: A filthy hanky lies by the roadside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dirty handkerchief' reads as one phrase, but 'dirty' is wordplay and 'handkerchief' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A foulard is a silk handkerchief or scarf, and also the light fabric it is made from.

clue.text: Female needing help across road? There’s warmth of affection

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for female
a lame person may need help to cross a road

explanation.surface: A woman being helped across the street shows how kindness warms the heart.
explanation.walkthrough: LAME is clued by a little scene rather than a synonym, which the question mark flags: someone lame may need a hand crossing the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A flame is a burning passion, the warmth of love; an old flame is a past sweetheart.

clue.text: Stream possibly for a teacher who is on the move

definitions.text: a teacher who is on the move

blocks.note: a stream that ripples and sparkles is said to be dancing, and it masters its course
reads as a teacher changing jobs, but means one whose subject is movement itself

explanation.walkthrough: A stream that sparkles and ripples is said to be dancing; the teacher whose lessons are all about moving is a dancing master.
explanation.definitionFit: A dancing master was a teacher of dancing, a profession whose whole business is movement.

clue.text: Is your setter game to be a friend abroad?

blocks.note: the setter speaking of himself asks 'am I'

explanation.surface: The setter asks whether he is up for being a pal overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your setter' is the crossword's author, I, so 'is your setter' turns into 'am I'. 'Game' looks like 'willing', but it is the board game GO.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Abroad' marks a foreign word: this is the Spanish for friend.

clue.text: Outdoor work done finally before pouring rain

indicators.note: 'Done finally' asks for the final letter of 'done'.
'Before' puts the work and E ahead of the rain.
Rain pouring down is tumbling about, so its letters are shaken up.

blocks.note: OP, short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Gardening work finished just before a downpour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outdoor work' looks like a single phrase, but 'Outdoor' alone is the definition and 'work' is OP.
explanation.definitionFit: Open-air means taking place outdoors.

clue.text: Lavatory sufficed, to be fair

blocks.note: 'can' is American slang for a lavatory

explanation.surface: A grudging verdict on a toilet: it did the job, to be fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To be fair' sounds like a throwaway phrase, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Candid means frank and even-handed, and 'to be candid' is close to 'to be fair' as a way of speaking plainly.

clue.text: We sit around being entertained by silly men offering story

indicators.note: Letters moved around are rearranged.
A guest entertained by a host is held inside the host's home.
Silly men are jumbled men, so MEN is rearranged.

blocks.note: letters to rearrange, which end up split around the other part

explanation.surface: People lounging with a bunch of foolish men who tell tales.
explanation.walkthrough: Unusually, both host and guest are jumbled: 'around' works on the first pair of words and 'silly' on the last, and only then does one go inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A news item is a single story in a newspaper or bulletin.

clue.text: On return the German female’s on phone creating diversion

indicators.note: Coming back means going the other way, so DER is read backwards.
HER is put on, next to, RING.

blocks.note: der is a German word for 'the'

explanation.surface: A returning German woman is on the phone, distracting everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The German' is not a person but the German article DER.
explanation.definitionFit: A red herring is something that diverts attention from the real issue.

clue.text: Moses stood on it completely pulverised, we hear

indicators.note: What we hear is what is said, not what is written.

blocks.note: wholly means completely and ground means pulverised

explanation.surface: A Bible scene where the ground under Moses is crushed to dust.
explanation.walkthrough: In Exodus, God tells Moses at the burning bush to take off his sandals, because the place he stands is holy ground.
explanation.definitionFit: The ground Moses stood on at the burning bush is called holy ground in the Bible.

clue.text: My word is given to supporter losing heart

indicators.note: IS is handed on to what follows, joining it.
Losing its heart, ALLY drops its middle letters.

explanation.surface: Someone promises their word to a friend who has lost courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing heart' means losing the middle, and for a four-letter word that is both central letters.
explanation.definitionFit: 'My word!' and 'I say!' are both exclamations of surprise.

clue.text: Someone to study heavenly body (or ‘glean sphere’ fancifully)

indicators.note: Arranged fancifully, the letters take a new, whimsical order.

explanation.surface: A stargazer who would rather glean a sphere than study it.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrase is pure fodder; it is not English, which is the giveaway that it should be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A selenographer studies the physical features of the Moon, a heavenly body.

clue.text: Old coins from countries with King or Queen engraved

indicators.note: What is engraved is cut into the surface, so R goes inside.

explanation.surface: Ancient money from various nations, stamped with a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: R serves for either monarch, as Rex or Regina, which is why the clue can say 'King or Queen'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stater was a gold or silver coin of ancient Greece.

clue.text: Stress over woman getting upset is something no one wants

indicators.note: In a down answer, getting upset means turning upside down, so DI reads ID.
ACCENT spreads over ID, covering it on both sides.

blocks.note: stress on a syllable is an accent

explanation.surface: Worry about an upset woman is unwelcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stress' looks like worry, but it is emphasis on a syllable, ACCENT.
explanation.definitionFit: An accident is an unwanted mishap that nobody wishes for.

clue.text: See 1
Cyclone had dislodged rocky stuff

indicators.note: Dislodged letters are knocked out of place.

explanation.surface: A storm has shaken loose rocks and debris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky stuff' seems to be what the cyclone moved, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Chalcedony is a waxy form of quartz, a mineral found in rock.

clue.text: Sort of yarn women kept in basket

indicators.note: W is kept inside the basket.

blocks.note: a creel is a wicker basket, used for fish

explanation.surface: Women's knitting wool is stored in a basket.
explanation.walkthrough: A creel is the angler's wicker basket.
explanation.definitionFit: Crewel is a thin worsted yarn used for embroidery.

clue.text: Close company having removed Ecstasy — and its pusher?

indicators.note: NEAR has E, for Ecstasy, taken out.

blocks.note: E is slang for the drug Ecstasy

explanation.surface: A firm shuts down after dropping a drug, and wonders about its dealer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close company' looks like shutting a business, but 'close' is NEAR. The definition leans on 'Ecstasy': 'its pusher' is the one who pushes the drug.
explanation.definitionFit: A narco is a drug dealer or trafficker, someone who pushes drugs such as Ecstasy.

clue.text: Become less severe about cook smelling

indicators.note: RELENT goes about, around, DO.

blocks.note: to relent is to become less severe
to do food is to cook it

explanation.surface: A cook with a strong smell is treated less harshly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' is a verb here: to do the vegetables is to cook them.
explanation.definitionFit: Redolent means smelling strongly, as in 'redolent of garlic'.

clue.text: See some in Paris weep

explanation.surface: An instruction to go and watch some people crying in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' reads as a cross-reference instruction, like 'See 1', but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though a literary one, meaning to catch sight of something far off.

clue.text: See 1
Irish poet of 21 drinking gallons

indicators.note: SYNE drinks G, taking it inside.

blocks.note: the answer to 21, the last word of AULD LANG SYNE

explanation.surface: An Irish poet from the past knocks back gallons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of 21' reads as 'of long ago', since syne means 'since', but it points to the entry SYNE.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Synge was an Irish poet and playwright, author of The Playboy of the Western World.

clue.text: Meet with ruin, not working

indicators.note: Letters working are being worked into a new shape.

explanation.surface: Facing disaster because something has broken down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not working' looks like one phrase meaning broken, but 'not' is fodder and 'working' alone is the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for an unplanned encounter: bumping into an old friend in the street.
